title: git flow: develop, release and hotfix branches
summary: Run a full git-flow cycle by hand: features onto develop, cut a release branch, stabilise it, ship it, then hotfix production — and merge everything back so nothing is lost.
mental_model: main is what is in production; develop is what is next. Everything else is temporary. The rule that keeps it consistent: every release and hotfix branch merges into BOTH main and develop, or a fix silently disappears at the next release.

steps.title: Two long-lived branches
steps.why: main holds exactly what is deployed, tagged at every release. develop holds the accumulating next version. Everything below branches from one of these and merges back into one or both.

steps.title: Two features onto develop
steps.why: Feature branches start from develop and merge back to develop — never to main. `--no-ff` keeps each feature visible as a unit in history, which is the point of the model.

verify.label: two features are on develop and not yet on main

steps.title: Cut the release branch
steps.why: `release/1.1.0` freezes the feature set. develop stays open for the version after next, while the release branch takes only stabilisation fixes — this parallelism is the whole reason the model exists.

steps.title: Work continues on develop while the release stabilises
steps.why: A commit lands on develop for the version after next. It must NOT reach this release — and because the release branch was cut, it cannot.

actions.run: git commit -q -a -m "Fix crash on zero dose found in QA"

steps.expect: No experimental.py on the release branch.

steps.title: Ship it: merge to main and tag
steps.why: main receives the release branch and gets the tag. This is the moment 'what is in production' changes, and the tag is what makes that moment findable forever.

verify.label: the release is tagged on main
next version's work did not ship

steps.title: Merge the release branch back into develop
steps.why: The QA fix was made on the release branch only. Without this merge it would vanish at the next release — the single most common git-flow mistake, and it fails silently.
commands: git merge --no-ff -m "Merge release/1.1.0 back into develop" release/1.1.0

verify.label: the QA fix reached develop
verify.hint: merge the release branch into develop as well as main

steps.title: Production breaks: hotfix from main
steps.why: A hotfix branches from main, not develop — develop contains unreleased work that must not ship. It then merges to both, exactly like a release branch.

actions.run: git commit -q -a -m "Handle a missing temperature reading"
git merge -q --no-ff -m "Merge hotfix/1.1.1 into develop" hotfix/1.1.1

verify.label: …and in develop, so the next release keeps it
verify.hint: a hotfix merges into BOTH main and develop

steps.title: Clean up and publish
steps.why: Delete the temporary branches, push both long-lived ones and the tags. What remains is two branches and a tag per release — a history anyone can read.
commands: git branch -d release/1.1.0 hotfix/1.1.1 feature/dosing feature/alerts

verify.label: the hotfix shipped to production
verify.hint: hotfix branches from main and merges back to main

verify.label: …and reached develop, so the next release will not regress it
the release branch's QA fix also reached develop
only the two long-lived branches remain

pitfalls: Forgetting to merge a release or hotfix branch back into develop loses the fix at the next release. It fails silently — nothing warns you.
git flow suits products with versioned releases and supported older versions. For a service deployed ten times a day, it is pure overhead — use trunk-based instead.
The `git-flow` command-line tool automates these merges but hides them. Understanding the branch topology matters more than the tool.
Long-lived develop branches drift from main. If the two diverge for months, every release becomes a merge conflict festival.
cheatsheet: publish both lines and the tags
